claims.claim: Federal laws enforced by the EEOC protect against workplace discrimination on several bases, but the applicable statute and its coverage conditions must be identified rather than assumed.
For many private employers, Title VII, the ADA, and GINA have a 15-employee/20-calendar-week coverage threshold, while the ADEA uses a 20-employee threshold; state or local law can also matter.

Title VII identifies race, color, religion, sex, and national origin in its employment-practice provision, and its disparate-impact provision is specifically structured around a particular practice and stated statutory conditions.

EEOC guidance describes disparate treatment as differing treatment because of a protected basis and disparate impact as a neutral test or selection practice that disproportionately excludes persons on a protected basis under Title VII's stated framework.

Available federal remedies depend on the statute, finding, discriminatory action, effect, proof, respondent, and other legal limits; EEOC describes examples including placement, back pay, benefits, policy changes, and in some intentional-discrimination cases compensatory or punitive damages.

EEOC filing time limits are not one universal deadline: the agency states a general 180-day period that may extend to 300 days in specified state or local-law settings, with different rules for age claims and federal-sector matters.
